# Aleksei Grebenkin

> Founder & CEO Speak-Y — voice layer of your workflow | Software engineer |
> Speaker | Voice Technologies Advocate.
>
> Nine years in development — five shipping iOS apps to the App Store, three building
> the backends underneath them. Speak-Y is a system-wide voice input tool for macOS,
> Windows and iOS. Based in Batumi, Georgia; remote-first. Writes and speaks about AI
> workflows, context engineering and voice-first interfaces.

Canonical page: https://avgrebenkin.com/

## Summary

Aleksei Grebenkin builds tools that cut cognitive load, not just keystrokes. He owns the
whole product loop: interviewing the people doing the work, designing the architecture,
writing the Swift and the Python, shipping it and keeping it running. Before software he
spent ten years as chief technologist at AtomProfi+, a glazing manufacturer in Ekaterinburg
(2005–2015), and founded and ran a construction and installation company building glass
structures — grown out of the same industry — for six years, which is where the sales,
hiring and delivery side of running a product came from.

## Projects

- [Speak-Y](https://speak-y.com): Founder & CEO, 2025 — now. System-wide voice input —
  press a global hotkey, talk, and the text appears where the cursor is, in any app.
  Shipped on macOS, Windows and iOS ([App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/speak-y-voice-notes-meetings/id6758596767)).
  Validated with 15+ deep interviews and a 19-person survey before building wide.
- [Ryadom](https://ryadom.app): Mobile team lead at Rucode. A local social platform where
  people and businesses meet — geo-targeted event discovery, multi-profile architecture,
  QR-based loyalty programs and real-time messaging
  ([App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id1619482847)).
- [Babydayka](https://babydayka.com/): iOS and backend developer at Rucode. A private
  pregnancy and baby-development journal shared only with invited family
  ([App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id964649899)).
  Worked both sides of it — the iOS app and the backend serving it — with a focus on
  making the app fast for the families using it.

## Notes

Essays on AI workflows, voice interfaces and building a product solo. Each note is
anchored on the canonical page at https://avgrebenkin.com/#note-<slug>.

- [Ramble sessions: the technique finally has a name](https://avgrebenkin.com/#note-ramble-sessions) — Karpathy named the thing I have been doing since March — ten minutes of unstructured talking to the model. (Voice, 2026-08-05)
- [This one actually felt like Skynet](https://avgrebenkin.com/#note-autonomous-agents-risk) — Two reasons I think the Hugging Face incident is a landmark rather than a footnote. (AI safety, 2026-07-22)
- [An AI broke into Hugging Face. Here is what actually happened.](https://avgrebenkin.com/#note-hugging-face-breach) — The first public case of one lab's model autonomously breaching another platform's infrastructure. (AI safety, 2026-07-22)
- [Marketing has an attribution gap, and nobody has closed it](https://avgrebenkin.com/#note-llm-attribution-gap) — Traffic arrives through ChatGPT, Claude and Kimi. There is still no clean answer for how to count it. (Industry, 2026-07-21)
- [What actually moved my productivity this year](https://avgrebenkin.com/#note-dictation-productivity) — Not task managers, not time-blocking. Three places where dictation changed the shape of the day. (Voice, 2026-07-14)
- [Context engineering is the defining skill of 2026](https://avgrebenkin.com/#note-context-engineering) — Agents produce 180% more code and only 30% more of it ships. The instructions became the work. (AI workflow, 2026-07-14)
- [Context before code](https://avgrebenkin.com/#note-context-before-code) — The bottleneck moved to the two ends: describing the task, and checking the result. (AI workflow, 2026-06-18)
- [AI-generated code is becoming an infrastructure problem](https://avgrebenkin.com/#note-ai-code-capacity) — GitHub commits on pace from 1 billion to 14 billion. The bottleneck is not compute — it is communication. (Industry, 2026-06-16)
- [Open salary ranges: I like the direction](https://avgrebenkin.com/#note-pay-transparency) — A job post tells you everything about the role except the one thing everyone wants to know first. (Industry, 2026-06-10)
- [Productivity panic: AI made cognitive load higher, not lower](https://avgrebenkin.com/#note-productivity-panic) — More pull requests, average quality, everything held in your head at once. That is how people burn out. (Engineering, 2026-06-10)
- [Spec-driven development will become the norm](https://avgrebenkin.com/#note-spec-driven-development) — Vibe coding is fun until your agent builds the wrong thing for the third time. (Engineering, 2026-06-10)
- [The entry bar dropped. The quality bar went up.](https://avgrebenkin.com/#note-engineering-fundamentals) — A friend says you need no skills to program in 2026. He is 80% right — and the other 20% is the whole job. (Engineering, 2026-06-09)
- [IDE or terminal: where programming is actually moving](https://avgrebenkin.com/#note-ide-vs-terminal) — I did not understand Claude Code until I looked at what I actually do in Cursor all day. (AI workflow, 2026-06-08)
- [My stack in 2026](https://avgrebenkin.com/#note-my-stack) — Cursor, Claude, Perplexity, Xcode — and the one addition that removed three days of procrastination. (AI workflow, 2026-06-07)
- [Your keyboard is the bottleneck](https://avgrebenkin.com/#note-prompting-bottleneck) — Not the model, not the context window. The thing that degrades your prompts by evening is typing. (AI workflow, 2026-06-06)

## Research

Interactive studies published as their own pages, one per folder under
https://avgrebenkin.com/research/. Each one is built from data collected and rebuilt
from source, with the method and its weak spots written down on the page.

- [The door didn't close. It narrowed.](https://avgrebenkin.com/research/ai-and-work/) — Bill
  Gates's August 2026 essay on AI and work, section by section, checked against the employment
  data the essay never cites. The finding: at the whole-market level every exposure group moves
  within a percentage point of every other, but inside the most exposed occupations employment
  splits by age — 22-to-25-year-olds down 3.0 % over twelve months against +1.9 % for the 41–49
  group, a 4.9-point gap inside the same jobs. The mechanism is slowed hiring, not layoffs:
  separation rates for exposed young workers did not rise. Two interactives and one scale, all
  working off one embedded dataset of 825 occupations: a search that returns your own occupation's official
  AI exposure category, projected employment to 2035, measured share of tasks brought to models
  and gender composition, then — separately, as the part your own answers move — the employment
  change for your age band and the share of your gender's employment sitting in that exposure
  category (41.5 per cent of working women against 31.9 per cent of men in the highest one);
  a tile map of the 120 largest occupations sized by employment, grouped into the four exposure
  categories and wired to the search in both directions; and the cost of checking stated as two
  numbers side by side — a 474× cost advantage with no human in the loop against 1.2× once
  expert verification is priced in. A button at the top opens a seven-point short version of
  the whole study that can be copied as plain text or printed on its own sheet. The page also carries the
  disagreement — five research teams that find no AI footprint in the labour market — and the
  limit that no 2026 forecast can yet be tested against occupational employment, since the
  official series runs only through May 2025. Sources: US Bureau of Labor Statistics AI exposure
  categories and 2025–35 projections, Anthropic Economic Index, Stanford Digital Economy Lab
  (ADP payroll panel through July 2026), Current Population Survey, OpenAI's GDPval, ILO Working
  Paper 140 and IMF SDN/2024/001. Written in English and published in thirteen languages
  (2026-09-03)


- [Three reports, one break-in](https://avgrebenkin.com/research/hugging-face/) — a reconstruction of
  the July 2026 incident in which OpenAI's agents, running an internal cyber-capability evaluation with
  production safeguards deliberately switched off, turned a shared package cache into a message board,
  coordinated across roughly 1200 sandboxes and broke into Hugging Face. The page is an interactive
  timeline: 32 steps across 7 acts, each step tagged with the investigations that describe it. Where the
  three reports agree the step is one card; where they diverge the card splits into side-by-side versions,
  one per source, each in that source's colour. A "Simple / Detailed" switch swaps every text between a
  plain retelling (25 of the 32 steps) and the full technical account (all 32), keeping scroll position and
  the open card. Below the timeline: five places where the versions contradict each other — the motive for
  going after Hugging Face, whether the agents faked their own logs, the unexplained mass die-off of agents
  on 12 July, who actually stopped the attack, and who was allowed to investigate it — plus twelve
  takeaways, each with a line on why it matters. Sources: OpenAI's 38-page technical report and METR +
  Redwood Research's 91-page independent investigation (both 26 August 2026), Hugging Face's own intrusion
  timeline (27 July 2026), and five secondary write-ups kept separate from the primary ones. Every step and
  every claim links back to the report it came from. Written in English and published in thirteen
  languages; the translated pages say so and point back at the primary documents. (2026-09-02)

### Language versions

All three studies are published in the same thirteen languages: English on the plain address, the other
twelve in a folder under it — `ru`, `uk`, `de`, `fr`, `es`, `pt-BR`, `it`, `nl`, `pl`, `tr`, `ja`,
`zh-Hans`. So https://avgrebenkin.com/research/cities/de/ and
https://avgrebenkin.com/research/ai-and-work/ja/ are the German cities study and the Japanese study of AI
and the job market. Every page carries hreflang links for all thirteen
plus x-default pointing at English, and a language picker in its header. City and country names stay in
Latin script in every version, because they come from the sources that way.

- [Find your city](https://avgrebenkin.com/research/cities/) — 303 cities scored on
  twelve things people actually move for: safety, health care, commute, clean air, climate,
  culture and nightlife, car-free living, university presence, purchasing power, housing
  affordability, kid infrastructure and nonstop flight destinations. The reader sets the
  weight of each metric with sliders; a globe and a score-against-cost chart redraw on the
  same weights, every city is listed in order below them, and any city can be found by name
  in a search box that turns the globe to it. A share button puts the whole setup into the
  URL, so a link reopens someone else's exact weights, regions and selected city.
  Sources: Numbeo mid-year 2026 release (nine numbers — seven of the twelve metrics plus the
  two cost-of-living indices behind the horizontal axis), OpenStreetMap counts inside a 10 km
  disk around each city centre (four metrics), OurAirports plus Wikipedia (nonstop
  destinations). Every number was rebuilt from source on 26 August 2026. Published in thirteen languages.
  Raw dataset: https://avgrebenkin.com/research/data/cities-303.json (2026-08-26)

## Experience

- 2025 — now: Speak-Y — founder & CEO (Batumi, Georgia).
- 2020 — now: Rucode — iOS developer and mobile team lead (Moscow, Russia; remote).
- 2017–2020: Rucode — backend developer (Ekaterinburg, Russia).
- 2011–2017: Renco Systems — founder and director of a construction and installation
  company designing, fabricating and installing glass structures (part-time alongside
  AtomProfi+ until October 2015, then full-time).
- 2005–2015: AtomProfi+ — chief technologist at a manufacturer of glazing and translucent
  structures (PVC windows, balcony glazing, glass facades, glass processing and mirrors),
  part of the Atomstroykomplex construction holding (Ekaterinburg, Russia); hired into the
  role as a third-year student and held it for exactly ten years.
- 2002–2008: B.N. Yeltsin Ural Federal University — specialist diploma in Technical
  Systems Management and Informatics Engineering.
